title: Jamming transition in an active exclusion process
abstract: Multiple studies on active matter have shown that activity can induce or suppress a phase transition, or modify the critical behavior of a passive system. Here we investigate how activity affects the jamming transition which is a paradigmatic example of nonequilibrium phase transitions in passive systems. We consider a one-dimensional system of active particles with hardcore interactions and a direction of self-propulsion which can be reversed at a given switching rate. For a class of particle hop rates and infinite switching rate, our model reduces to a passive system which is known to exhibit a transition between a high-density fluid phase and a low-density jammed phase in the stationary state. Using Monte Carlo simulations and a mean field theory, we study how the mean mobility of the particle and the hole cluster distribution vary with density and finite switching rate. Our main result is that activity hinders the formation of jam and can even inhibit it; more precisely, we find that the jamming transition occurs at a critical density that decreases with decreasing switching rate, and at sufficiently small switching rate, the system exists only in the fluid phase.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes the jamming transition in an active 1D particle system where particles self-propel and randomly reverse direction. Using Monte Carlo simulations and Mean Field Theory, the authors show that activity actively resists jamming, causing the critical density for jamming to drop as activity increases. This suggests a fundamental control mechanism over phase transitions using external driving forces.
main_problem: The study investigates how introducing activity (self-propulsion with switching) affects the jamming transition, a key non-equilibrium phase transition in passive particle systems.
main_result: Activity generally hinders or can completely inhibit the formation of a jammed state; specifically, the critical density for jamming decreases as the switching rate decreases, potentially keeping the system fluid even at high densities.
method: The research employs both Monte Carlo simulations to study time evolution and Mean Field Theory (MFT) to derive steady-state equations for particle distributions and mean mobility.
model_or_system: The model is a one-dimensional ring of hard core particles where each particle has an internal binary variable ($\eta = \pm 1$) determining its self-propulsion direction, which switches at rate $	ilde{\gamma}$.
key_observables: Mean mobility ($w$), the critical jamming density ($ho_c$), and the distribution functions of hole clusters ($P^{\alpha eta}_n$).
important_parameters: Particle density ($ho$), switching rate ($	ilde{\gamma}$ or $\gamma$), and a hopping parameter $b$. Key regimes include the passive limit ($	ilde{\gamma} 	o \infty$) and the small activity limit ($	ilde{\gamma} 	o 0$).
main_assumptions: The Mean Field Theory approach ignores spatial correlations between sites, and certain analyses rely on perturbation theory or specific scaling limits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate mean particle mobility ($w$) versus density ($ho$) and switching rate ($\gamma$), showing agreement with passive models at high $\gamma$ and summarizing the phase diagram (Fluid/Jammed).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the active system dynamics to applying MFT for steady-state analysis. It then analyzes limiting cases: large $\gamma$ (approaching passive behavior), small $\gamma$ (high activity), and finally, a scaling limit ($ho/\gamma$ finite) to derive asymptotic behaviors.
why_interesting: The work provides theoretical insights into how non-equilibrium driving forces modify fundamental phase transitions, which has parallels in understanding active matter systems relevant to biological or synthetic physical contexts.
